clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic variants in DDHD2, which encodes the principal intracellular phospholipase A1 and triglyceride lipase of the brain.
Very early onset, often in infancy or the first years of life, with spastic paraplegia together with global developmental delay and intellectual disability.
Highly characteristic clue: an abnormal lipid peak on brain proton MR spectroscopy, reflecting neuronal triglyceride and lipid accumulation from failed lipid hydrolysis.
Brain MRI commonly shows a thin corpus callosum with periventricular white-matter signal change and sometimes cerebral or cerebellar atrophy.
Additional features include dysarthria, strabismus, foot deformities, short stature and, in some, dystonia or seizures.
The MR-spectroscopy lipid signal distinguishes SPG54 from most other complicated spastic paraplegias and, when present, strongly suggests a DDHD2 defect.
SPG54 belongs to the DDHD-domain phospholipase group of spastic paraplegias; DDHD1 (SPG28) is its closest sibling gene.
reference.pathophysiology: DDHD2 encodes DDHD domain-containing protein 2, an intracellular phospholipase A1 that also possesses triacylglycerol lipase activity and is regarded as the main enzyme hydrolysing triglycerides within the central nervous system; it localises to the Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum and to lipid droplets, participating in membrane phospholipid remodelling and lipid-droplet turnover. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause pathological accumulation of triglycerides and lipid droplets within neurons, detectable as an abnormal lipid peak on MR spectroscopy, and disrupt membrane lipid homeostasis. The consequence is length-dependent corticospinal degeneration accompanied by cognitive impairment and white-matter change.
additionalDifferentials: SPG28 (DDHD1) — the sibling phospholipase gene and closest biochemical mimic
SPG11 (spatacsin) and SPG15 (spastizin) — early-onset complicated forms with thin corpus callosum and cognitive impairment
SPG35 (FA2H), SPG56 (CYP2U1) and SPG46 (GBA2) — other lipid-metabolism complicated spastic paraplegias
Spastic diplegic cerebral palsy, a common early misdiagnosis given the young age at onset
Primary leukodystrophies presenting with early spasticity and white-matter change
additionalInvestigations: Gene panel or exome sequencing to confirm biallelic DDHD2 variants with family segregation
Brain MRI with proton MR spectroscopy, specifically seeking an abnormal lipid peak
Assessment of corpus callosum thickness and periventricular white matter on MRI
redFlags: Failure to thrive or short stature warranting paediatric review
reference.prognosis: The disorder is early in onset and slowly progressive; intellectual disability is usual and many children have significant motor disability, but the course is chronic rather than rapidly fatal.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosis as cerebral palsy because of the very early onset and apparently static early course
Not requesting MR spectroscopy and thereby missing the diagnostic lipid peak
Attributing the white-matter change to a primary leukodystrophy
Overlooking recessive inheritance and the need for family testing
references: Hereditary spastic paraplegia clinical and genetic reviews
management: Symptomatic antispasticity therapy with baclofen or tizanidine, and botulinum toxin for focal spasticity
Physiotherapy, stretching, orthoses and orthopaedic care for foot deformities and contractures
Anti-seizure medication if seizures occur and anti-dystonic therapy where dystonia is present
Developmental, educational and speech-and-language support for the intellectual disability and dysarthria
Ophthalmological and orthoptic review for strabismus
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with carrier testing of relatives
Multidisciplinary paediatric neurology, rehabilitation and ophthalmology input
